rationale: B wins because it is a little more disciplined about shooting its own weak claims before a reporter does. A's "Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" invents a competitive battlefield the update does not supply, while B admits "Honestly weak as a standalone time hook" on the residency angle and asks for a real peg. Both sets are useful, but B also finds a real use for offline-first instead of leaving it as a rejected bare feature.
gaps_in_A: "Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" is unsupported. The update gives no incumbent names, displacement, bake-off, or competitive response.
"major banks piloting a tool historically seen as too lightweight for their compliance bar" is plausible color, not supplied fact. Make it a question or require an outside source.
A mostly wastes the offline-first fact. Refusing "Notion ships offline-first editing" is right, but the set never builds a stronger workflow-continuity or SaaS-architecture angle from it.
The EU/Australia residency angle treats launch timing as enough. Without a regulatory peg or named blocked buyer, it is slower compliance context, not a strong pitch.
gaps_in_B: "cleared the hardest security review in the market" overclaims. A pilot is not a full deployment or proof that bank security has signed off.
"after it added customer-held encryption keys" implies sequence and causality the update does not prove. CMEK may be connected, but the angle needs bank-side confirmation.
"will pay for control, not features" is sloppy against the supplied fact that there is no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans. The story is adoption control, not paying more.
"cloud-only collaboration tool" and the whole "reversal" frame require proof of Notion's prior architecture and the market orthodoxy. B flags the risk, but the headline still leads with it.
